 MINNEAPOLIS — For the first time since having knee surgery, which is slated to knock him out for more than 2 months, Minnesota Timberwolves star Anthony Edwards met with the media ahead of his team's matchup against the defending champion New York Knicks on Thursday.
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement "I think they're playing great," said Edwards, who appeared to be in good spirits despite the long rehabilitation process he is in the midst of enduring. "Great team ball. Ayo's playing phenomenal. Rudy's playing great. Melo's getting everybody involved, and then Jaden is stepping up big time. I think they're playing great."
 Edwards has been sidelined since October 27th with the aforementioned arthroscopic cleanup surgery that took place on October 29th. The Timberwolves maintained an eight-and-three record in his absence. 
 Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) 
 When asked if he believes the NBA should consider shortening the length of the season, as it could be attributed to a large increase in soft tissue injuries, Edwards said, "I don't really care, man. I'm cool with 82, I'm cool with 92, it don't bother me. I don't care."
 Edwards has a different theory as to why there has been such a stark increase in this caliber of injuries, to him and notable stars such as Pacers guard Tyrese Haliburton, Warriors guard Stephen Curry, and Trailblazers guard Ja Morant. "I think the thing is the game is just so fast now, it's just up and down, up and down, up and down," said the Atlanta native. "There's really no half-court time now, so you don't really get no time to rest until timeouts." 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement In the 2025-2026 season, Edwards averaged 35.0 minutes per game in 61 games played, good for ninth throughout the association. 
 His teammate, and the undisputed most health-conscious member of the Timberwolves, Rudy Gobert agreed with Edwards' assessment, but has an elaborated theory as to why there is such an uptick in soft-tissue injuries.
 Click Here to Subscribe "I mean, the pace … I don't have the exact numbers, but the number of possessions, you know, 700 minutes, is much higher than it used to be, right. So, much more cutting. … I think the way we train has to do something with that too. And so it's up to the debate, but I think the way we lift weights — I think back then guys were lifting much more, much heavier … I think that's great for your body. I think that's great for your tendons, for tissues, and that's something we need to do more around the league. The plyometrics and all that is great also, but I think both are very important."
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement While Gobert gave his unfiltered, honest, and informed stance on the matter, he did note that he is not a licensed medical professional. "I'm not a doctor, I'm not a scientist," he said. "I am very curious about these things, and I think, you want my opinion? I think (lack of heavy weight lifting) plays a big part of it, too."
